stem: A die is rolled 4 times. The probability of getting a six on any single roll is 1/4. What is the probability of getting at least one six in 4 rolls?

per_option_rationale.rationale: Computing P(X=0) = (3/4)^4 = 81/256 and stopping, reporting the complement event instead of the required event.
Computing only P(X=1) = C(4,1)(1/4)(3/4)^3 = 4 × (1/4) × (108/256 (equal to 27/64)) = 27/64, treating 'at least one' as 'exactly one'.
Computing P(X=4) = (1/4)^4 = 1/256, treating 'at least one six' as 'a six on every roll'.

explanation:
1. Direct addition of all cases with one or more sixes is tedious. Use the complement.
2. P(no six in 4 rolls) = (3/4)^4 = 81/256.
3. KEY STEP: P(at least one six) = 1 - 81/256 = 175/256.
4. The complement method is the efficient route for 'at least one' binomial problems.

explanation_sections.punchline: "At least one" is fastest solved by complement. P(no six in 4 rolls) = (3/4)^4 = 81/256, so P(at least one) = 1 - 81/256 = 175/256.
explanation_sections.approach: Model: Binomial(n=4, p=1/4). Assumptions: rolls are independent; p is given as 1/4. Decisive move for any 'at least one' question: compute P(X=0) = q^n instead of summing all cases with X >= 1. Here q = 3/4, so P(X=0) = (3/4)^4 = 81/256. Subtract from 1 to get the answer. Summing P(X=1)+P(X=2)+P(X=3)+P(X=4) directly gives the same result but takes four times as long.
explanation_sections.lesson: "At least one" always translates to 1 - P(none). Apply this reflex immediately: write q^n, subtract from 1, done. Trying to count each success case individually is the slow path and wastes exam time.
explanation_sections.timing: 60-90 seconds. Reject option (1) = 1/256 in 5 seconds: that is (1/4)^4, the probability of all four rolls showing a six. Reject option (3) = 81/256 in 5 seconds: that is P(no six), the complement you computed, not the event asked.
